Monitoring with BDRIBS: contour plots, sensitivity and pooled trials

Source: vignettes/bdribs-monitoring.Rmd
bdribs-monitoring.Rmd
library(bssd)

Waterhouse et al. (2022) describe how a safety management team uses BDRIBS (vignette("bdribs1")) in ongoing blinded trials: a contour plot of the posterior probability \(P(RR > 1)\) over the numbers of events and the patient-years of exposure prepared before the first patient enters the trial, a sensitivity analysis over the background rate, and pooling of blinded data from several trials with different randomization ratios. The examples use a fixed background rate and the Jeffreys prior Beta(0.5, 0.5) for \(p\).

Contour plot

Example 1 of Waterhouse et al. (2022): MACE with a background rate of 3.1 events per 100 patient-years and randomization 1:1.

g <- bdribs_grid(y = 4:10, exposure = seq(40, 240, by = 10),
                 lambda_hp = 0.031, p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
z <- matrix(g$prob, nrow = 7)
contour(4:10, seq(40, 240, by = 10), z, levels = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9),
        xlab = "Number of events", ylab = "Patient-years of exposure")

The probabilities for six and seven events (Figures 3 and 4):

subset(g, y %in% 6:7 & exposure %in% c(80, 100, 140))
#>    y exposure lambda_hp      prob
#> 31 6       80     0.031 0.9037555
#> 32 7       80     0.031 0.9649264
#> 45 6      100     0.031 0.8076505
#> 46 7      100     0.031 0.9128135
#> 73 6      140     0.031 0.5678571
#> 74 7      140     0.031 0.7324799

Sensitivity to the background rate

With 10 events in 200 patient-years, the probabilities at the limits of the 90% credible interval of the background rate from 496 events in 15,730 patient-years (Figures 5 and 6) are

bg <- qgamma(c(0.05, 0.95), 496, 15730)
bdribs_grid(y = 10, exposure = 200, lambda_hp = bg, p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
#>    y exposure  lambda_hp      prob
#> 1 10      200 0.02923996 0.8654598
#> 2 10      200 0.03389652 0.7554039

The background rate can also be given a Gamma prior instead of a fixed value (pt_hp in bdribs_post()).

Pooled trials

Example 3: trial A with 250 patient-years at 1:1 and trial B with 80 patient-years at 2:1 are pooled; the effective randomization ratio is the ratio of the expected exposures on study drug and on control.

k <- pooled_ratio(c(250, 80), c(1, 2))
k
#> [1] 1.175824
bdribs_post(y = 16, exposure = 330, k = k, lambda_hp = 0.031, pt_hp = Inf,
            p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.9101
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.905, median 1.846, 95% interval (0.6727, 3.469)

Reproduction of Waterhouse et al. (2022)

inst/reproduce/reproduce_Waterhouse2022.R compares the probabilities, exposures and the pooled randomization ratio given in the text and figures (11 PASS, 1 FAIL). The published values were read from an R Shiny application that samples by MCMC; the tolerance is 0.01 for probabilities given in percent and 0.02 for those given as “about” (the other tolerances are in the table).

P(RR > 1), 10 events, 200 PY, upper limit of the background rate 0.76 0.755 0.020 PASS

References

Waterhouse, B., Hartford, A., Mukhopadhyay, S., Ferguson, R. and Hendrickson, B. A. (2022). Using the Bayesian detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data (BDRIBS) method to support the decision to refer an event for unblinded evaluation. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 21(2), 372–385. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2175
